A commenter on a thread about B200 vs H200 benchmarks (GEMM throughput, distributed training, LLM inference) said simply: "B200 is indeed much better than H200."
The engineer who virtualized NVIDIA HGX B200 GPUs said the hardest part was handling NVLink: it complicates isolation while trying to preserve performance.

Complaint about the HGX B200 software stack: NVIDIA's Fabric Manager is not open source but is required to bring up and manage the NVLink/NVSwitch fabric on HGX systems. A commenter disputed the "open source" framing, and the author conceded it "isn't a fully open GPU stack."

On multi-tenant isolation for HGX B200, the implementer chose Shared NVSwitch Multitenancy mode. Fabric Manager programs NVSwitch routing tables so GPUs in different partitions can't exchange NVLink traffic, and each VM gets exclusive GPUs via VFIO passthrough. He noted this relies on NVIDIA's documented mechanisms and is not equivalent to AWS's threat model.

The implementer said they deliberately avoided NVIDIA vGPU on B200. They used whole-GPU and NVSwitch-partitioned passthrough instead, as a better fit for their workloads that need to preserve NVLink bandwidth.
Workaround described for B200 passthrough: allocate at the IOMMU-group level rather than per device, passing through all devices in the group. This avoids partial-passthrough problems.

A commenter noted that MIG devices are hard to pass into KVM VMs. The team they worked with didn't believe it was possible and suggested switching to VMware, because the MIG interface gives a UUID rather than a PCI BDF. Another user replied that a MIG-backed vGPU mode via SR-IOV can work, though it still needs host software.
A reader puzzled over the blog's note that each GPU's BAR mmaps 256 GB per GPU and worried it would waste about 2 TB of RAM. They then realized it consumes address space, not RAM.

Asked about infiniband inside VMs in Shared NVSwitch mode, the author said they hadn't looked deeply at inter-machine communication yet. He said NVLink/NVSwitch are intra-node, so InfiniBand comes down to NIC passthrough, NUMA/PCIe placement and validating RDMA inside the VM.
